title: The Native American City That Rivaled Medieval London
tags: cahokia, illinois, mississippian, native american history, mounds
script: Around the year 1100, a major city stood across the river from today's St. Louis. Cahokia, in Illinois, was built by the Mississippian culture. At its peak, as many as twenty thousand people may have lived there, and some scholars think it rivaled London at the time. Its centerpiece, Monks Mound, is a hundred-foot earthen mound covering about fourteen acres. By 1350, the city was abandoned. Its mounds still rise today.

title: The Astronomer With a Metal Nose and a Pet Elk
tags: tycho brahe, astronomy, eccentrics, renaissance
script: One of history's greatest astronomers wore a metal nose. In 1566, Danish nobleman Tycho Brahe lost part of his nose in a sword duel with his cousin, after a quarrel over who was the better mathematician. He wore a replacement for the rest of his life. Modern tests suggest it was brass. He also kept a tame elk. According to one account, it drank too much beer at a dinner and fell down the stairs. Science was wild.

title: Thumbs Down Probably Didn't Mean Death
tags: gladiators, ancient rome, thumbs down, myths
script: Thumbs down meant death for a gladiator. Except, historians aren't sure it did. Roman writers mention a turned thumb deciding a fighter's fate, but they never clearly say which way it turned. Some scholars even think a thumbs up may have signaled death. So why do we all picture thumbs down? A French painting from 1872 called Pollice Verso made the idea famous, and it later inspired the movie Gladiator. Our signal came from an artist.

title: A Plane's Last Message Was a Word No One Understands
tags: star dust, stendec, andes, aviation mystery
script: In 1947, an airliner crossing the Andes sent one strange final word in Morse code: STENDEC. The Star Dust was flying from Buenos Aires to Santiago with 11 people aboard. Then it vanished. Searchers found nothing. Starting in 1998, wreckage began emerging from a glacier on Mount Tupungato. The plane had most likely flown into the mountain in heavy cloud and snow. Mystery partly solved. But STENDEC? Nobody knows what it meant.

title: It Might Rain Diamonds on Neptune
tags: neptune, uranus, diamonds, space
script: On Neptune and Uranus, it might rain diamonds. These icy giant planets contain methane, which is made of carbon and hydrogen. Thousands of kilometers below their clouds, crushing pressure and heat may squeeze that carbon into diamonds that slowly sink deeper inside. In 2017, scientists at SLAC fired powerful lasers at plastic to recreate those conditions, and tiny nanodiamonds formed in an instant. On the real planets, they could grow much bigger. Forecast: brilliant.

title: When Americans and Germans Fought Side by Side
tags: castle itter, world war two, 1945, austria, strange battles
script: In May 1945, American and German soldiers fought on the same side. At Castle Itter in Austria, the Nazis had held famous French prisoners, including two former prime ministers and a tennis star. When SS troops attacked, a small American tank crew, German army soldiers led by an anti-Nazi major, and the prisoners themselves defended the castle together. The tennis star slipped out to bring help. Reinforcements arrived. The prisoners went home.

title: 33,000 People Lived on Just Six Acres
tags: kowloon walled city, hong kong, density, lost places
script: Imagine more than thirty thousand people packed into about six and a half acres. That was Kowloon Walled City in Hong Kong. Because of a quirk in an 1898 lease, neither Britain nor China really governed it. Its buildings stacked up to about fourteen stories, capped by flight paths into a nearby airport. Sunlight barely reached the narrow alleys. The city was torn down in the early 1990s. Today, it's a peaceful park.

title: America's Richest Woman Was Called a Witch
tags: hetty green, wall street, eccentrics, gilded age
script: She was the richest woman in America, and newspapers called her the Witch of Wall Street. Hetty Green turned an inheritance into a fortune estimated at over one hundred million dollars by 1916. Her strategy was simple: buy undervalued assets and hold them. During the Panic of 1907, she lent money to New York City. Yet she dressed in plain black and lived in cheap rented rooms. Guinness once called her the world's greatest miser.

title: Knights Didn't Need Cranes to Mount Horses
tags: knights, medieval armor, myths, middle ages
script: Knights did not need a crane to get onto their horses. A full suit of field armor usually weighed about forty-five to fifty-five pounds, less than a firefighter's breathing gear, spread across the whole body. Most knights could put a foot in the stirrup and climb on. One French marshal reportedly climbed the underside of a ladder in full armor, using only his hands. The crane myth started as a joke and was popularized by a 1944 movie.

title: Eight Letters on a Monument Nobody Can Decode
tags: shugborough inscription, codes, england, unsolved
script: On an English estate, eight carved letters have puzzled people for over 250 years. The Shepherd's Monument at Shugborough Hall was built in the mid-1700s. Under a copy of a Poussin painting sit the letters O U O S V A V V, with D and M below. Is it a love note? A Bible verse? A treasure clue? Even former Bletchley Park codebreakers took a look. One historian says it's just graffiti. Nobody has proven anything.

title: Mars Has a Volcano the Size of Arizona
tags: olympus mons, mars, volcano, space
script: The largest volcano in the solar system is on Mars, and it's the size of Arizona. Olympus Mons rises sixteen miles above the surrounding plains, more than twice the height of Mount Everest above sea level. It stretches about 370 miles across. Yet its slopes are so gentle that standing on it would feel like a slowly rising plain. Low gravity and a hot spot that stayed put let lava pile up for ages. Too big to notice.

title: The WWII Submarine Sunk by Its Own Toilet
tags: u-1206, submarine, world war two, toilet, naval history
script: In 1945, a German submarine was brought down by its own toilet. U-1206 had a new high-pressure toilet that crew were supposed to operate with trained help. Off the coast of Scotland, after the commander used it, the wrong valve was opened. Seawater rushed in and reached the batteries below, releasing toxic chlorine gas. The submarine had to surface, where it was spotted and attacked. Most of the crew survived, as prisoners.

title: Egypt's Legendary Port Was Found Under the Sea
tags: thonis-heracleion, sunken city, egypt, underwater archaeology
script: For centuries, this Egyptian port was known mostly from ancient writers like Herodotus. Then, in 2000, divers found it under the sea. Thonis-Heracleion lies in Abu Qir Bay near Alexandria, about four miles offshore. Archaeologists led by Franck Goddio have recovered large statues, gold coins and around seventy ancient ships. After floods and quakes, the ground beneath the city gave way, and the sea moved in. A lost city, hiding underwater.

title: The WWII Officer Who Carried a Sword and Longbow
tags: jack churchill, world war ii, eccentrics, bagpipes
script: One British officer went into World War Two carrying a sword. Jack Churchill, nicknamed Mad Jack, was also a skilled archer with a longbow, and appeared briefly in the 1940 film The Thief of Bagdad. He reportedly said any officer who goes into action without his sword is improperly dressed. During a 1941 commando raid in Norway, he played the bagpipes as the landing ramps came down. A medieval warrior in a modern war.

title: The King Who Gave Away So Much Gold It Lost Value
tags: mansa musa, mali empire, medieval africa, gold
script: One king gave away so much gold that he lowered its value. In 1324, Mansa Musa, ruler of the Mali Empire, passed through Cairo on his pilgrimage to Mecca. He handed out gold to officials all over the city. According to the historian al-Umari, so much gold flooded Cairo that its price fell, and it still hadn't recovered twelve years later. The twist? On his way home, Mansa Musa reportedly had to borrow money.

title: The Bloop: The Ocean Sound That Fooled Everyone
tags: bloop, ocean sounds, noaa, mystery solved
script: In 1997, underwater microphones in the Pacific picked up a sound so loud it reached sensors thousands of miles apart. Scientists nicknamed it the Bloop. It was ultra-low and rose in pitch over about a minute. Some people wondered whether a gigantic sea creature made it. But it was far louder than any known animal. In 2005, NOAA researchers found the real source: an icequake, an iceberg cracking off Antarctica. The monster was made of ice.

title: Butterflies Fly to a Place They've Never Been
tags: monarch butterfly, migration, insects, nature
script: Every fall, monarch butterflies fly to Mexico, a place none of them have ever been. Summer monarchs live only a few weeks. As they spread north, several generations are born, one after another. Then, at summer's end, a special super generation emerges. These butterflies can live up to eight months, eight times longer than their parents. They fly up to three thousand miles to the same wintering grounds their ancestors left. No map. No guide. Just instinct.

title: The Newspaper That Picked the Wrong President
tags: dewey defeats truman, 1948 election, harry truman, newspaper, presidents
script: In 1948, a major newspaper announced the wrong winner for president. Polls almost unanimously predicted Thomas Dewey would beat President Harry Truman. A printers' strike forced the Chicago Daily Tribune to go to press hours early, before most results were in. So it printed a giant headline: Dewey Defeats Truman. Truman won. Days later, a grinning Truman held up that very paper for photographers. It became one of history's most famous photos.

title: Easter Island's Heads Have Hidden Bodies
tags: easter island, moai, rapa nui, archaeology, statues
script: Easter Island's famous heads are not just heads. Many of the moai on the slopes of the Rano Raraku quarry are buried up to their shoulders in soil and quarry debris. Excavations have shown full torsos below ground, some with markings linked to traditional Rapa Nui tattoos. More than nine hundred moai are known, mostly carved between about 1250 and 1500. The faces got famous. The bodies were hiding underneath.

title: The Magic 8 Ball Began as a Fortune Teller's Tool
tags: magic 8 ball, toys, odd origins, fortune telling
script: The Magic 8 Ball started with a fortune teller. In Cincinnati, Albert Carter was inspired by a spirit writing device his mother, a clairvoyant, used. He built a sealed cylinder with answers floating inside. Sold as the Syco-Slate, it flopped. A crystal ball version didn't do much better. Then in 1950, a billiards company ordered a version shaped like a pool eight ball. That one took off. Ask again later.

title: Two Monks Smuggled Silkworms Into Byzantium
tags: silk road, byzantine empire, justinian, smuggling
script: One of history's greatest heists was pulled off by two monks with walking sticks. For centuries, China guarded the secret of how silk was made. Then, in the sixth century, two monks who had seen silk production made a deal with the Byzantine emperor Justinian. They traveled back east and returned with silkworm eggs hidden inside hollow bamboo canes. That smuggled cargo launched Byzantium's own silk industry. The secret of silk was stolen in a stick.

title: The Island Hole Treasure Hunters Can't Stop Digging
tags: oak island, money pit, treasure, nova scotia
script: For over two centuries, people have been digging into one small island in Nova Scotia. In 1795, according to legend, a teenager named Daniel McGinnis spotted a strange depression on Oak Island. Later diggers reported layers of logs underground. Then the shaft flooded with seawater. Pirate gold? Lost treasure? Vast fortunes have been spent searching. Scientists point to natural sinkholes and tides flooding the pit. Still the digging goes on. The treasure has never appeared.

title: This Frog Freezes Solid and Comes Back to Life
tags: wood frog, alaska, animals, winter
script: In Alaska, there's a frog that freezes every winter, and survives. The wood frog can let up to sixty percent of its body turn to ice. Its heart stops beating. Its breathing stops. It can stay that way for months. Its secret is sugar. The frog floods its cells with glucose, which works like antifreeze and protects them. When spring arrives, it thaws, its heart starts again, and it hops away. Nature's greatest comeback story.

title: Teddy Roosevelt Got Shot, Then Gave His Speech
tags: theodore roosevelt, 1912, bull moose, assassination attempt, presidents
script: In 1912, Theodore Roosevelt was shot in the chest, and then he gave his speech anyway. Campaigning in Milwaukee, the former president was hit by a would-be assassin's bullet. It was slowed by his steel glasses case and a folded fifty-page speech in his coat pocket. Roosevelt told the crowd, 'It takes more than that to kill a Bull Moose,' and kept talking. Doctors left the bullet in place. He carried it for life.

title: The Ancient Stone City Built on the Sea
tags: nan madol, micronesia, pohnpei, megaliths, lost city
script: Just off a Pacific island's shore sits a city built on the sea itself. Nan Madol, on Pohnpei in Micronesia, is made of nearly one hundred artificial islets, linked by tidal canals. Its walls are stacked from massive basalt columns brought from across the island. It was the seat of the Saudeleur dynasty, which ruled Pohnpei for centuries. Legend says two sorcerers flew the stones there. Archaeologists say people built it over generations.

title: Britain Has a Law Against Handling Salmon Suspiciously
tags: strange laws, salmon act, united kingdom, fishing
script: In Britain, you can be prosecuted for handling salmon in suspicious circumstances. That's the real heading of section 32 of the Salmon Act 1986. It sounds like a joke, but the purpose is serious. It targets anyone who receives, hides or moves salmon when they believe, or should suspect, it was caught illegally. Think of it as handling stolen goods, but fishier. Penalties can reach two years in prison. Very fishy business indeed.

title: The First Labor Strike Was in Ancient Egypt
tags: ancient egypt, labor strike, ramesses iii, valley of the kings
script: The first recorded labor strike happened over three thousand years ago in Egypt. Around 1158 BC, under Pharaoh Ramesses the Third, the skilled workers who carved the royal tombs in the Valley of the Kings weren't getting their grain rations. So they put down their tools. They marched, staged sit-ins at temples, and complained loudly, shouting that they were hungry. And it worked. The grain was released. The men building eternity for pharaohs walked off the job.

title: The Abandoned Ship That Drifted for 38 Years
tags: baychimo, ghost ship, arctic, alaska
script: A cargo ship abandoned in the Arctic kept turning up for 38 years with no one aboard. In 1931, the Hudson's Bay Company steamer Baychimo got trapped in sea ice off Alaska. Part of the crew camped nearby. Then a blizzard hit. When it cleared, the ship was gone. They assumed it had sunk. It hadn't. People spotted it drifting for decades, the last time in 1969. Where is it now? Nobody knows.

title: This Blue Planet Rains Glass in 5,400 MPH Winds
tags: exoplanet, hd 189733b, space, astronomy
script: About sixty-four light-years away is a deep blue planet that looks peaceful. It isn't. HD 189733b is a giant planet about the size of Jupiter, whipping around its star every 2.2 days. Its blue color doesn't come from oceans. It comes from hazy clouds laced with silicate particles. Scientists think it rains molten glass there, in winds up to 5,400 miles per hour, about seven times the speed of sound. Beautiful from far away. Deadly up close.

title: Both Guns Misfired, So Andrew Jackson Grabbed His Cane
tags: andrew jackson, 1835, assassination attempt, davy crockett, presidents
script: The first known attempt to kill a US president ended with the president charging his attacker. In 1835, outside the Capitol, a man aimed a pistol at Andrew Jackson. It misfired. He pulled out a second pistol. That one misfired too. The 67-year-old Jackson went after him with his walking cane. Bystanders, including Congressman Davy Crockett, helped subdue the man. An expert later put the odds of both guns failing at 125,000 to one.
